planting.note: Plant divisions or small starts in spring into very well-drained, gritty alpine soil in full sun, giving light afternoon shade where summers are hottest; Gold Nugget is among the most cold-hardy of all ice plants, tolerating winter lows well below zero where drainage stays sharp.

directions: Gold Nugget forms an unusually tight, dense alpine mat of tiny succulent leaves that stays under a few inches tall, making it one of the lowest-profile hardy ice plants for crevice and rock gardens. From a South African high-elevation population, it is exceptionally cold hardy compared to most Delosperma, surviving winters that kill tender ice plant species outright, though it appreciates a bit more regular moisture and afternoon shade in scorching summer climates than lowland relatives like Delosperma cooperi. Foliage takes on maroon and rust tones through winter before a heavy spring flush of shining, deep-yellow, daisy-like flowers covers the mat. Use it between paving stones, in gravel scree beds, or as a very low edging where standing winter moisture, not cold, is the main threat to its survival.
sources: Plant Select (Denver Botanic Gardens / Colorado State University)
Ontario Rock Garden and Hardy Plant Society

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light part sun; Starburst was selected from seed collected by plantsman Panayoti Kelaidis in South Africa's Free State and is a benchmark Plant Select ice plant introduction.

directions: Starburst covers itself from early summer into fall with bright lavender-pink to lilac-purple flowers, each with a crisp white eye at the center and petals that shimmer with the metallic-flecked sheen typical of ice plant foliage. It forms a low, dense mat of succulent leaves well suited to rock gardens, dry slopes, and container culture, tolerating both full sun and light afternoon shade better than many hardy Delosperma selections. As with other cold-hardy ice plants, winter wet rather than cold temperatures is the main cause of decline, so sharp drainage is essential for reliable perennial survival. It needs almost no deadheading or feeding once established, flowering heavily on minimal supplemental water through the hottest part of summer.
sources: Plant Select (Denver Botanic Gardens / Colorado State University)

planting.note: Plant divisions or small starts in spring into lean, very well-drained soil in full sun; Sutherland ice plant is less reliably cold-hardy than Delosperma nubigenum or congestum and needs sharp winter drainage to persist as a perennial in colder zones.

directions: Sutherland ice plant forms a low, spreading mat of fleshy, evergreen succulent leaves studded from early to midsummer with masses of small, starry, pink to magenta-purple flowers accented by a bright yellow center. It is native to the Drakensberg region of South Africa and Lesotho and is somewhat less bombproof through winter wet than the toughest hardy ice plants, so in climates with cold, soggy winters it is often grown as a short-lived perennial or treated as an annual rather than a permanent groundcover. Give it the sharpest possible drainage — a gravel-mulched slope, raised bed, or rock garden crevice — and avoid any irrigation or mulch that keeps the crown moist during dormancy. Where conditions suit it, established mats reward minimal care with a long, heavy midsummer bloom that draws bees steadily to the flat, sun-loving flowers.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Shirokunshi Lotus (Tulip Lotus, White Single-Petal Bowl Lotus)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally in heavy clay soil in a wide, shallow, undrained container submerged just below the water surface in full sun once water has warmed; Shirokunshi, known in the trade as Tulip Lotus, is a compact, free-flowering white bowl lotus popular for container water gardens.

directions: Shirokunshi produces slightly fragrant, single, pure-white flowers with narrow, upright petals that stay cupped in a distinctive tulip-like form rather than opening flat, held above rounded blue-green leaves from early to late summer. Scaled between the truly miniature bowl lotus cultivars and full-sized pond lotus, it is compact enough to bloom reliably in a half-barrel or wide tub without the acreage a large-flowered lotus like Mrs. Perry D. Slocum demands. Feed with aquatic plant fertilizer tablets through the growing season, and in zones with hard winter freezes, sink the container below the pond's ice line or move it to a frost-free space, since lotus tubers are damaged by hard freezing. Divide congested tuber banks every two to three years in early spring, discarding old woody sections and replanting only firm, plump tips.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Perry's Super Star Lotus (Large Color-Changing Double Pink Lotus)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally in heavy clay soil in a large, wide, undrained container or directly in a pond bottom submerged a few inches below the water surface in full sun; Perry's Super Star is a large, vigorous lotus bred by Perry D. Slocum that needs generous room to reach its full size.

directions: Perry's Super Star bears enormous, richly double flowers with more than fifty petals that open pink, shift through pink-and-yellow tones over the following days, and finally fade to a soft cream, so a single planting displays several flower colors across its bloom cycle. Among the first lotus cultivars to bloom each year, it grows tall and vigorous on sturdy stems and needs a large, deep container — at least 30 to 48 inches across — or an open pond bottom to reach its full stature, making it unsuitable for small tub culture. The bold, rounded, blue-green leaves rise well above the water, and flowering continues from early to late summer once the water has warmed. Divide overcrowded tuber banks every few years in early spring, and in cold-winter climates lower the container below the pond's ice line or move it to frost-free storage over winter.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Charles Thomas Lotus (First US-Patented Lotus Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally in heavy clay soil in a wide, undrained aquatic container submerged a few inches below the water surface in full sun; Charles Thomas was bred by Perry D. Slocum and named for Charles B. Thomas of Lilypons Water Gardens, and was the first lotus ever awarded a US plant patent.

directions: Charles Thomas produces lavender-pink flowers that soften to a paler lavender-pink as they age, carrying a faint, sweet licorice-like fragrance that sets it apart from many other lotus cultivars, held above broad, blue-green leaves on a medium-sized plant well suited to a half-barrel, large tub, or small pond. Bred by noted hybridizer Perry D. Slocum and released in the 1980s, it was historically significant as the first lotus cultivar ever granted a United States plant patent, a milestone in ornamental aquatic plant breeding. It tolerates a wide range of water depths over the growing tuber and blooms reliably from early to late summer once the water has warmed past danger of frost. Feed with aquatic fertilizer tablets through the growing season, and protect the container from hard freezing in winter by sinking it below the pond's ice line or moving it to frost-free storage.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society
